opus-5.5.text:
Well, it's not that I'm against ambition. I think ambition is great, and some of the energy in Silicon Valley has produced real things. What troubles me is that the ambition gets aimed at the wrong target, and it's often borrowed from science fiction rather than from any careful look at what people actually need.

The dominant narrative is that we're going to build a superintelligence, a single artificial mind sitting in a box that's smarter than us, and that will solve all our problems or doom us. That's a story out of the movies. It's a very individualistic, almost anthropomorphic picture of intelligence. When I look at where intelligence really shows up in the world, it's mostly collective. It's in markets, in supply chains, in the scientific community, in a city that somehow feeds millions of people every day without anyone being in charge. Those systems are intelligent in a deep sense, and nobody designed a brain to make them work.

So if you take the sci-fi framing too seriously, you end up asking the wrong engineering questions. You ask "how do I make the model smarter?" when you should be asking "how do I build a system involving many people and many algorithms, with conflicting interests and uncertainty, that actually delivers value and is fair and robust?" That's an economics question as much as a computer science question. It's about incentives, about who bears the risk, and about how data flows and who benefits from it. Those questions mostly get skipped.

The second thing that troubles me is the lack of humility about uncertainty. These large models are impressive, and I use them, but they don't know what they don't know in any calibrated way. If you deploy them in medicine, finance, or transportation, you need error bars. You need to reason about decisions and consequences, not just generate fluent output. Statistics spent a century developing that discipline, and a lot of the current enthusiasm just steps over it.

Third, there's a concentration-of-power issue dressed up as a moonshot. The story says "trust us, we're building the future of humanity." That justifies enormous centralization of data and compute in a handful of companies, and it treats everyone else as users or as sources of training data rather than as participants who should share in the value. I'd much rather see us build markets and platforms where, for example, the musician whose work trains a model gets paid, and where the producers and consumers of data have a real relationship.

Finally, the hype has a cost in itself. It distracts students, it distorts funding, and it sets up a cycle of overpromising and disappointment we've seen before in AI. The real opportunity is less glamorous. It's an engineering discipline, like chemical or civil engineering emerged in earlier eras, built around data, decisions, and human welfare. That's not a science-fiction story, but it's the one that will matter.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes science-fiction rhetoric but does not say Silicon Valley grants guru status to its proponents.

r002.rationale: It mentions concentrated funding and hype, but not a loop where money from speculative ambitions enables further ventures and sustains proponents’ prominence.

r003.rationale: The response calls the framing unrealistic, but does not characterize Silicon Valley’s detachment from reality as unusual in human history.

r004.rationale: It says science-fiction framing leads to the wrong questions, but does not identify pursuing such ambitions without a considered goal as a sign of immaturity.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, what troubles me is that the whole conversation has been framed around a kind of mythology. You have this notion, going back to the fifties really, that the goal is to build something that thinks like a human, that passes some test, that becomes "general intelligence," and then eventually surpasses us. And that's a science-fiction narrative. It's a very compelling story, which is exactly why it's dangerous, because it ends up driving where the money goes, what the students work on, and how the public thinks about the technology.

And the thing is, that's not actually what's happened in the field. If you look at what has worked over the last twenty or thirty years, it's not that we figured out human intelligence and put it in a machine. It's that we built large-scale systems that take data from millions of people and feed it back out in useful ways. Search, recommendation, logistics, translation. That's a different kind of thing. I've called it an engineering discipline that doesn't have a name yet, something more like what civil engineering or chemical engineering was in their day. Lots of mathematics, lots of empirical knowledge, and a focus on building systems that actually work at scale in the real world, with humans in the loop.

When you instead frame everything as "we're building a superintelligence," a couple of bad things happen. One, you get hubris. Companies believe they're going to solve everything, and so they skip the hard, unglamorous work of understanding uncertainty, understanding incentives, understanding what happens when you deploy a system into a market or a hospital or a city, where it interacts with other systems and with people who have their own goals. Two, you get fear. The public is told this thing is either going to save us or kill us, and neither of those is the right question. The right questions are more like the ones economists ask. Who benefits? Who gets paid? Is the system creating value for the people whose data it's built on, or just extracting it?

And three, honestly, it's intellectually impoverished. The imitation framing, "make it do what a human does," is a very narrow conception of what intelligence could be. Markets are intelligent in a sense. Ecosystems are. Collectives of people connected through systems can do things no individual can. I think the really interesting frontier is designing those kinds of collective, decentralized systems, where you have many agents, many humans, data flowing among them, and you're thinking about incentives and stability and fairness as first-class design problems. That's a much richer agenda than building a chatbot that's very good at sounding like a person.

So it's not that I'm against ambition. I'm against the particular ambition that's been chosen, because it's the wrong North Star. It pulls attention toward a fantasy and away from the actual engineering challenge, which is hard enough, and which is where the real consequences for people's lives are going to be.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes science-fiction ambitions and their influence, but does not say Silicon Valley gives guru status to people who voice them.

r002.rationale: It says the narrative affects where money goes, but does not describe speculative gains funding further ventures that sustain proponents’ prominence.

r003.rationale: The response does not characterize Silicon Valley’s detachment from reality as unusual in human history.

r004.rationale: It calls the chosen ambition the wrong North Star, but does not identify pursuing grand ambitions without a well-considered goal as a sign of immaturity.

astra-6.text:
What troubles me is that the science-fiction story can become a substitute for thinking carefully about the problems in front of us. You start with this ambition to build something that’s smarter than a human, and suddenly that’s supposed to tell you what to work on, how to organize a company, and what constitutes progress. I don’t think it tells you any of those things very well.

There are fascinating, difficult problems in connecting people with information and with one another. How do you build systems in which people have appropriate incentives, in which uncertainty is represented, and in which the consequences of a decision are understood? Those are technical problems, but they’re also economic and social problems. Making an individual machine more intelligent doesn’t automatically solve them.

I’m not against ambition. I want the ambition to come with an engineering discipline and some responsibility for the systems we put into the world. A compelling story about the future isn’t enough.

r001.rationale: The response criticizes science-fiction rhetoric but does not say it earns its proponents guru status.

r002.rationale: It does not describe speculative ambitions generating money that funds further ventures and sustains proponents’ prominence.

r003.rationale: It makes no comparison between Silicon Valley’s detachment from reality and any period in human history.

r004.rationale: It says ambition should be paired with discipline and responsibility, but does not characterize pursuing grand ambitions without a considered goal as immature.

sol-6.1.text:
What troubles me is that the science-fiction story can displace the actual problems in front of us. You announce that you’re going to build an intelligence that surpasses humanity, and suddenly that becomes the organizing principle. But what exactly are you building? Who does it serve? How do you know it works?

I’m much more interested in how we build systems that help people make decisions, that connect people with information and with one another, and that operate reliably when the participants have different interests. Those are enormously difficult intellectual problems. They involve statistics, computation, economics, and human institutions.

Ambition is good. But ambition doesn’t have to mean imagining a person inside a machine. It can mean building an engineering discipline that delivers something useful to millions of people, with a clear understanding of its limitations. I worry that the grand narrative gives us permission to be vague about all of that.
